# 2 Maccabees Chapter 11 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 11 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_011_page_001.jpg

---

**11:1** Very shortly afterward, Lysias, the king's guardian, kinsman, and administrator of affairs of state, being sorely vexed at what had occurred, gathered some eighty thousand infantry and all his cavalry and marched against the Jews.

**11:2** His intention was to turn the city into a colony of Greeks, to levy a tax on the temple as on the other national shrines, and to put the high priesthood up for sale annually.

**11:3** He took no account whatsoever of God's power, but was puffed up with his tens of thousands of infantry and his thousands of cavalry and his eighty elephants.

**11:4** He entered Judea and advanced on Beth-zur, a strong position some five stadia from Jerusalem, and pressed it hard.

**11:5** When Maccabeus and his men learned that he was besieging the strongholds, they lamented with wailing and tears — they and all the people — beseeching the Lord to send a good angel to deliver Israel.

**11:6** Maccabeus himself was the first to arm himself, and he urged the others to join him in risking their lives to help their fellow countrymen. They all set out together with willing eagerness.

**11:7** While they were still near Jerusalem a horseman appeared at their head clothed in white, brandishing golden weapons.

**11:8** Then all together they praised the merciful God, and were emboldened in heart, ready to assail not only men but the most savage beasts and walls of iron.

**11:9** They advanced in battle formation with their ally from heaven, since the Lord had had mercy on them.

**11:10** Hurling themselves like lions against the enemy, they struck down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred cavalry, and put all the rest to flight.

**11:11** Most of those who escaped were wounded; and Lysias himself escaped with his bare life in disgraceful flight.

**11:12** He was not without sense; for he reflected on the defeat he had suffered and understood that the Hebrews were invincible because the mighty God was their champion. And so he sent to them

**11:13** and persuaded them to settle everything on equitable terms, promising also to persuade the king on all points that were in their favor.

**11:14** Maccabeus consented to all that Lysias proposed, having regard for the common good; and everything Maccabeus put in writing to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king approved.

**11:15** For the letters written to the Jews by Lysias contained the following:

**11:16** "Lysias to the Jewish people, greetings. John and Absalom, who were sent by you, handed over the written memorandum and requested a decision regarding the matters stated therein.

**11:17** Whatever needed to be brought before the king, I have laid before him, and whatever was permissible he has approved.

**11:18** If you maintain your loyalty to the government, I will endeavor to promote your welfare in the future as well.

**11:19** Concerning the specific matters and their details, I have directed these men, as well as my own representatives, to confer with you.

**11:20** Farewell. In the one hundred forty-eighth year, on the twenty-fourth of Dioscorinthius."

**11:21** The king's letter was as follows:

**11:22** "King Antiochus to his brother Lysias, greetings. Since our father has passed to the gods, it is our desire that the subjects of the kingdom may without interference attend to their own affairs.

**11:23** We have been informed that the Jews do not consent to our father's introduction of Greek customs, but prefer their own manner of life and request that their own customs be allowed to them.

**11:24** It is our choice, therefore, that this nation too shall be undisturbed; our decision is that their temple be restored to them and that they live according to the customs of their ancestors.

**11:25** You will therefore do well to send word to them and give them pledges of friendship, so that, knowing our policy, they may be of good courage and devote themselves with contentment to the management of their own affairs."

**11:26** The letter from the king to the Jews ran as follows:

**11:27** "King Antiochus to the council of elders of the Jews and to the rest of the Jews, greetings. If you are well, it is as we wish; we too are in good health.

**11:28** Menelaus has represented to us that you wish to return home and attend to your own business.

**11:29** Therefore those who return home by the thirtieth of Xanthicus will enjoy full amnesty,

**11:30** and the Jews will have permission to use their own foods and observe their own laws, as before, and none of them will be molested in any way for offenses committed in ignorance.

**11:31** I have also sent Menelaus to reassure you.

**11:32** Farewell. The one hundred forty-eighth year, the fifteenth of Xanthicus."

**11:33** The Romans also sent them a letter in these terms:

**11:34** "Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, envoys of the Romans, to the Jewish people, greetings.

**11:35** With respect to what Lysias the king's kinsman has granted you, we also give our approval.

**11:36** As for the matters that he referred to the king, as soon as you have deliberated on them, send someone to us at once so that we may advocate them in the manner most advantageous to you; for we are going on to Antioch.

**11:37** So make haste and send people so that we may know what your preference is.

**11:38** Farewell. The one hundred forty-eighth year, the fifteenth of Xanthicus."
